description_full: Choice Hotels International, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, operates as a hotel franchisor in the United States and internationally. It operates through Hotel Franchising & Management and Corporate & Other segments. The company franchises lodging properties under the Comfort Inn, Comfort Suites, Quality, Clarion, Clarion Pointe, Sleep Inn, Ascend Collection, Econo Lodge, Rodeway Inn, MainStay Suites, Suburban Studios, WoodSpring Suites, Everhome Suites, Cambria Hotels, Radisson Blu, Radisson RED, Radisson, Park Plaza, Country Inn & Suites by Radisson, Radisson Inn & Suites, Park Inn by Radisson, Radisson Individuals, and Radisson Collection brand names. The company was founded in 1939 and is headquartered in North Bethesda, Maryland.
ceo_bio: Mr. Dominic E. Dragisich | President, CEO & Director | Age 43 | Compensation: $1.7M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $910K ranks in the top quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, with revenue growing 7%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $132K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $22K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: Choice Hotels International, In is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $5.3B market cap on $1.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 22% against a 7% cost of capital — a 15-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $232M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.73× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.7× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.9×.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 40% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 3.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 28% operating margin runs 21pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $34.52 (margin of safety -244%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 21%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $20.37 to $55.46 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 26.4 vs 18.8, EV/EBITDA 15.5 vs 10.7 and P/FCF 22.8 vs 16.7 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-7%).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 17 covering analysts target $117 on average, 1% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 22% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 15pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.59).
It converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.73x.
ROE of 204% is amplified by 16.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 2.4% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.7x net debt to EBITDA ($45.0M of cash against $1.9B of debt), with interest covered 4.9x.
The current ratio of 0.87 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.4% over 3 years, 15.6% over 5 years and 6.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
At current returns, reinvesting 11% of profits supports about 2.5% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 24.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00 and a backlog worth 14% of annual revenue.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (2.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 28, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 39.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 77%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $1.4M sold).
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (2.6% in buybacks and 1.0% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 4.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 22 consecutive years, raising it 16.2% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 27.5% of the float, 9.9 days to cover.
people: With about 1,754 employees, each generates about $910K of revenue, 2.4x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 6.8% a year across its filed history.
